• **No sensory or cognitive** involvement and no diarrhea.
• *Clostridium botulinum* strains produce different types of toxins.
• Among them (A, B, C1, C2, D, E, F, and G) only **C2 IS enterotoxic**, while the rest are neurotoxins.

question_stem.text: Botulism causes
question_stem.markdown: Botulism causes

peer_accuracy_statement: 87% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Botulism causes **bilateral descending flaccid paralysis.**

Botulinum toxin acts by blocking the production and release of Acetylcholine at the synapses and neuromuscular junction.

The differential diagnosis of adult botulism cases include Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), myasthenia gravis, stroke syndromes, Eaton–Lambert syndrome, and tick paralysis.

• **Occasional GBS** cases present as the **Miller–Fisher variant**, whose characteristic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia is easily mistaken for the early descending paralysis of botulism. (But, **remember** that typically and commonly, GBS presents as **ascending** flaccid paralysis only.) Protein levels in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in GBS. **CSF findings are generally normal** in botulism.
• The edrophonium (Tensilon) test is sometimes of value in distinguishing botulism (usually a negative result) from myasthenia gravis (usually a positive result)
• In most cerebrovascular accidents, physical examination reveals asymmetry of paralysis and upper motor neuron signs. Brain imaging can reveal the rare basilar stroke that produces symmetric bulbar palsies
• Eaton–Lambert syndrome usually manifests as proximal limb weakness in a patient already debilitated by cancer.

question_stem.markdown: A veterinarian develops an ulcer with central black eschar over the forearm, the most probable causative organism is :

peer_accuracy_statement: 78% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
The most probable causative organism from the given clinical scenario is ***Bacillus anthracis*.** Human anthrax presents in one of three ways - Cutaneous, pulmonary, or intestinal.

**Cutaneous Anthrax:**
• It begins 2–5 days after infection as a small papule that develops within a few days into a vesicle filled with dark bluish black fluid.
• Rupture of the vesicle reveals a **black eschar** at the base, with a very prominent inflammatory ring of reaction around the eschar. It is referred to as a malignant pustule.
• The lesion is classically found on the hands, forearms, or head and is painless. The disease used to be common in dock workers carrying loads of hides and skins on their bare backs and hence was known as the 'hide porter's disease.'

**Pulmonary Anthrax (Wool sorter's disease)**
• It occurs in people who handle raw wool, hides, or horsehair and acquire the disease by inhalation of spores.
• This is a hemorrhagic pneumonia with a high fatality rate. Hemorrhagic meningitis may occur as a complication.

**Intestinal Anthrax:**
• It occurs mainly in primitive communities who eat the carcasses of animals dying of anthrax.
• An individual may suffer after a day or so from hemorrhagic diarrhea, and dies rapidly from septicemia.

**Treatment**

**Ciprofloxacin** is the recommended antibiotic.

In case of potential exposure, prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin or doxycycline should be given for 60 days and three doses of vaccine (AVA BioThrax).

Large **mucoid colonies** and a **positive string test** are suggestive of hypervirulent *Klebsiella pneumoniae* (hvKP).

• Classic *Klebsiella pneumoniae* (cKP)
• Hypervirulent *Klebsiella pneumoniae* (hvKP)

**hvKP** is an emerging variant from Asia and the Pacific Rim.

• The colonies tend to have **hypermucoviscous phenotype** and give a **positive string test.**
• Often presents as a **pyogenic liver abscess** in patients lacking a history of hepatobiliary disease.
• **The propensity for metastatic spread to distant sites** e.g., eyes, CNS, and lungs.

**Important infections** caused by hvKP:
• Necrotizing fasciitis
• Meningitis
• Brain abscess
• Endophthalmitis

peer_accuracy_statement: 88% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Plague is transmitted by rat flea.

• Plague is a **zoonotic disease.**
• The **plague bacillus** is a natural **parasite in rodents.**
• Infection is transmitted among them by **rat fleas.**
• The fleas acquire the infection by feeding on infected rodents.
• **In the flea, the bacilli multiply** in the stomach to such an extent that they **block the proventriculus.**
• The interval between the ingestion of the infected blood and blocking in the proventriculus is the **extrinsic incubation period, which is usually about 2 weeks** in *Xenopsylla cheopis*.
• When such a blocked flea bites another rodent, it cannot suck in blood because the bacterial mass blocks the passage mechanically.
• The blood, mixed with the bacteria is **regurgitated into the bite**, transmitting the infection.
• Infection may also be transferred by contamination of the bite wound with the feces of infected fleas.
• When a diseased rat dies (**rat fall**), the fleas leave the carcass and, in the absence of another rat, may bite human beings causing bubonic plague.
• Several species of **fleas** may act as **vectors**, the most important being *Xenopsylla cheopis, Xenopsylla astia*, and *Ceratophyllus fasciatus*.

images.visual_description: Photograph of seven cotton-plugged test tubes containing Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) agar slants arranged side by side, illustrating uninoculated control, alkaline/alkaline, alkaline/acid, alkaline/acid with black H2S precipitate, and acid/acid with gas reactions.

explanation_markdown:
*Salmonella* and *Shigella* produce a colorless colony in the eosin methylene blue agar because they **do not** ferment lactose.

EMB agar: Eosin methylene blue (EMB) agar is a selective, differential medium.

It is **selective** because it allows the growth of gram-negative rods and inhibits the growth of gram-positive organisms.

Its **differential** property is based on the fact that ***Salmonella* and *Shigella* do not ferment lactose** while other enteric gram-negative rods do.

On EMB agar, ***Escherichia coli* appear as dark blue-black colonies with green metallic sheen** because they are lactose fermenters.

Since both ***Salmonella* and *Shigella* appear colorless**, triple-sugar iron agar is used to differentiate *Salmonella* from *Shigella*.

This medium contains
• 0.1% glucose
• 1% sucrose
• 1% lactose
• Ferrous sulfate (for detection of H2S production)
• Tissue extracts (protein growth substrate)
• A pH indicator (phenol red)

It is poured into a test tube to produce a slant with a deep butt and is inoculated by stabbing bacterial growth into the butt.

If only glucose is fermented, the slant and the butt initially turn yellow from the small amount of acid produced; as the fermentation products are subsequently oxidized to CO2 and H2O and released from the slant and as oxidative decarboxylation of proteins continues with formation of amines, the slant turns alkaline (red).

• If lactose or sucrose is fermented, so much acid is produced that the slant and butt remain yellow (acid). *Salmonella* and *Shigella* typically yield an alkaline slant and an acid butt.
• If gas is produced, bubbles and cracks can be seen in the medium.
• If H2S is produced, the black color of ferrous sulfide can be seen.

explanation_markdown:
The test shown in the above image is **String test** performed to identify the colonies of *Vibrio cholerae*.

**Principle**
• The bacterial cells of ***Vibrio cholerae* are lysed by sodium deoxycholate**, causing the suspension to **lose its turbidity.**
• The **DNA released** from the lysed cells causes the mixture to become **viscous.**
• Thus, a **“mucoid string”** is formed when the inoculating loop is drawn slowly away from the suspension.

**Procedure**
• A loopful of growth is mixed with a drop of **0.5% sodium deoxycholate**/sodium taurocholate in saline on a slide.
• The loop is slowly pulled away from the slide.
• The appearance of **mucoid string** when the loop is slowly pulled upwards indicates **positive test result.**

explanation_markdown:
Cholera toxin causes continued activation of adenylate cyclase

• **Cholera toxin** activates the **adenylate cyclase enzyme** in cells of the **intestinal mucosa** leading to increased levels of **intracellular cAMP**, and the secretion of water, Na+, K+, Cl-, and HCO3- into the lumen of the small intestine.
• When cholera toxin is released, it binds to the intestinal cells through the interaction of the **pentameric B subunit of the toxin** with the **GM1 ganglioside receptor** on the intestinal cell, triggering endocytosis of the toxin.
• Cleavage of the **A1 domain** from the **A2 domain** occurs in order for A1 to become an active enzyme.
• Once inside the enterocyte, the enzymatic **A1 fragment** of the **toxin A subunit** enters the cytosol, where it activates the **G protein Gsa** through an **ADP-ribosylation** reaction that acts to lock the G protein in its GTP-bound form, thereby **continually stimulating adenylate cyclase to produce cAMP.**
• The **high cAMP levels** activate the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (**CFTR**), causing a dramatic efflux of ions and water from infected enterocytes, leading to watery diarrhoea.

The mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins are as given below:

1. Adenylate cyclase

• Edema factor (Bacillus anthracis)
• Exotoxin Y (Pseudomonas aeruginosa)

2. ADP-Ribosylation
• Cholera toxin (Vibrio cholerae)
• Heat-labile toxin (Escherichia coli)
• Diphtheria toxin (Corynebacterium diphtheriae)
• Exotoxin A (Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
• Pertussis toxin (Bordetella pertussis)
• C2 toxin and C3 ADP-ribosyltransferase (Clostridium botulinum)

3. Deamidation
• Cytotoxic necrotizing factor (Escherichia coli)
• Dermonecrotic toxin (Bordetella pertussis)

4. Glucosylation
• Toxin A and B (Clostridium difficile)

5. Metalloproteinase
• Lethal factor (Bacillus anthracis)
• Enterotoxin (Bacteroides fragilis)
• Botulinum neurotoxin (Clostridium botulinum)
• Tetanus neurotoxin (Clostridium tetani)

6. RNA glycosidase
• Shiga toxin (Shigella dysenteriae)
• Shiga-like toxin (Escherichia coli)

Cyclic AMP inducers ("CAPE")
• Cholera toxin => ADP-R of Gs
